questions.q: Why does Gowdy say questions are such an effective tool for persuasion?
a: They keep the focus on the other person and reduce defensiveness
They let you present facts faster than speeches
They make your opponent feel intellectually inferior
They allow you to avoid stating your own opinion
questions.why: Lesson 1 explains that good questions turn the exchange into a conversation instead of a confrontation.

questions.q: Which kinds of words does the summary warn against using in an argument?
a: Sweeping ones like everyone, never, and always
Technical terms your audience may not know
Emotional words that reveal how you feel
Questions that begin with why
questions.why: Lesson 2 says broad generalisations invite easy rebuttals, so your language should be precise.

questions.q: What does repetition achieve in a persuasive argument?
a: It makes the audience feel the point's importance
It gives you time to think of new points
It wears the other person down emotionally
It makes your argument sound more objective
questions.why: Lesson 2 notes that the more a point is repeated, the more weight the audience gives it.

questions.q: What is repackaging an opponent's argument?
a: Restating it so that it sounds absurd
Summarising it more fairly than they did
Combining it with your own strongest point
Repeating it back to them word for word
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes repackaging as rewording a claim until it appears ridiculous, as with the abuse example.

questions.q: Why does playing the victim work as a last-resort tactic?
a: People are naturally more sympathetic to victims
It makes your opponent lose their temper
It shifts the argument onto safer ground
It forces the other side to apologise
questions.why: Lesson 3 admits the tactic lacks dignity but works because audiences feel more empathy for victims.
